clue.text: This takes off appearance with some skill

parts.note: an air is a person's manner or outward appearance
craft means skill or expertise

explanation.surface: Someone shows off a polished look along with a certain talent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This takes off' looks like part of the sentence about someone's manner, but it is the definition: a thing that takes off from a runway. 'with some' simply joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A plane is the thing that leaves the ground at take-off, so the phrase describes a flying machine.

clue.text: Like to include animals for some clues

indicators.note: to include means the word for 'like' wraps around the animals

parts.note: as means like, in the sense 'as good as'
a nag (horse) and a ram (male sheep) are both animals

explanation.surface: A request to add creatures to a set of puzzle hints.
explanation.walkthrough: 'animals' gives two animals side by side, NAG and RAM, which sit inside AS.
explanation.definitionFit: Clues whose letters are rearranged form a familiar type of crossword clue, so these are one sort among many.

parts.note: red stands for a Russian, from the Soviet era
an ensign is a junior officer

explanation.surface: A Russian army man is seconded to headquarters staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staff' reads as personnel, but here it is a flagpole: the Red Ensign is the British merchant navy's flag.
explanation.definitionFit: A flag is fixed to a pole, and the British merchant navy's red flag is one such banner.

clue.text: A puzzling thing in the car hire business

indicators.note: in means the letters run inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Something baffling goes on at a car rental firm.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 'hiRE BUSiness'.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture puzzle of letters and symbols is a riddle, a thing that puzzles.

explanation.surface: Some forward-looking crooks.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who forge ahead are pushing onward, and those who forge documents are fraudsters.

parts.note: reads as a remorseful traveller, but means a magazine official who sends back unwanted manuscripts with a note of regret

explanation.surface: A man who wishes he had never come home.
explanation.walkthrough: A rejection slip says the publication 'regrets' it cannot use the piece, and the manuscript is returned.
explanation.definitionFit: A journal's chief sends rejected work back with polite regrets, so this person returns pieces with regret.

indicators.note: breaks down means the letters of the next words fall apart and are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wrongdoer collapses in tears following a duel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaks down' looks like the offender weeping, but it is the anagram signal working on the two words after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who fails to pay a debt or appear in court is a wrongdoer in breach of an obligation.

explanation.surface: A Dickens character tops up his dish.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver Twist famously holds out his bowl for more, but the bowl here is a pipe's: twist is a kind of rolled tobacco.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver of the orphanage novel is a Dickens hero, and a rolled tobacco plug is what a smoker packs into a pipe.

explanation.surface: A wordplay instruction about the name of a seaside town.
explanation.walkthrough: To re-sort letters is to make an anagram; Brighton is a seaside town on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Shuffling letters again means sorting them a second time, and a coastal holiday town is a place people go on holiday.

annotationWithheld.why: Cuts the old devil aboard: SNICKS is NICK (Old Nick, the devil) inside SS, but 'aboard' alone must both supply SS (steamship) and signal the container, one word doing two jobs

clue.text: Star baled out by the island group

indicators.note: out means the letters of the word beside it are put out of order

parts.note: the Aran Islands are a group off the west coast of Ireland

explanation.surface: A celebrity is bailed out by a band of islanders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'baled out' looks like a pilot's escape, but 'out' rearranges BALED to make ALDEB; 'by' joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Aldebaran is the bright red giant in the constellation Taurus, a named celestial body.

explanation.surface: Someone thwarts plain-speaking assailants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blunt' reads as outspoken, but it describes fencing swords with a button on the tip.
explanation.definitionFit: To frustrate a plan is to thwart it, and fencers' practice swords have blunted points.

clue.text: Old characters hasten to take French art

parts.note: to run is to hasten
es is French for 'art' as in 'thou art', the verb form

explanation.surface: Someone rushes off to collect some French paintings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'art' is the old verb 'thou art', not painting: French 'tu es'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient Germanic letters carved in stone are early alphabet symbols, old written characters.

indicators.note: half means only part of the word for 'when' survives, its second pair of letters

parts.note: then means at that time, when
a counter is the bar at which drinks are served

explanation.surface: Asks what happens when half the drinkers gather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' keeps only the second half of THEN, giving EN. 'the bar' looks like the drinkers, but it is the counter itself.
explanation.definitionFit: To come across someone or face them is to meet them.

clue.text: Understatement confuses someone, is the conclusion

indicators.note: the conclusion means the little word 'is' comes at the end
confuses means the letters of the following word are muddled

parts.note: split as 'some' plus 'one', with one giving I, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: Downplaying things baffles a person, so the finding goes.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'someone' as SOME + ONE (I); 'confuses' rearranges SOMEI to MEIOS, and 'is the conclusion' adds IS at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Meiosis is the rhetorical figure of deliberately playing something down, the opposite of hyperbole.

clue.text: Takes salary to dance? He's crazy!

parts.note: screw is old slang for wages or salary
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: Someone spends their pay on a dance and is thought mad.
explanation.walkthrough: SCREW is British slang for wages; 'Takes' and 'to' simply join the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A screwball is an eccentric, zany person, an oddball.

clue.text: Lot of people get let off by bench

parts.note: a set is a group of people

indicators.note: off means the letters of the next word are disturbed

explanation.surface: A crowd lets someone off beside a courtroom bench.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges LET to TLE; 'get' and 'by' are joining words.
explanation.definitionFit: A settle is a long wooden seat with a high back, a kind of bench.

clue.text: See the drink comes about four — and hurry up !

parts.note: to look is to see

indicators.note: comes about means the drink goes round the number

parts.note: ale is a drink, beer
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Watch the beer arrive around four o'clock, and be quick about it.
explanation.definitionFit: The order to move briskly urges someone to get a move on.

indicators.note: about means the jumbled letters go around the facial feature
confused means the letters of the word beside it are jumbled

parts.note: the chin is a facial feature

explanation.surface: Someone becomes muddled over a film about a face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' rearranges GETS to ETGS, and 'about' wraps those letters around the facial feature.
explanation.definitionFit: Prints made from engraved plates are artworks, images on paper.

parts.note: a grid is a framework of bars

explanation.surface: A young woman spotted in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bars' looks like pubs but means a grating, GRID; 'seen' joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingrid is a female given name, as in Ingrid Bergman.

clue.text: Someone refusing an old foreign coin ?

explanation.surface: A person turning down an antique coin from abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: One who says no or contradicts is a refuser, and a French penny of old was the denier.

clue.text: Prove to be in the assembly

explanation.surface: Seeming to belong in the gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that end up a certain way prove so, and the crowd who attend an event make up the gathering.

parts.note: reads as a satisfied Dormouse, but means what fills a well in the Dormouse's story at the Mad Hatter's tea party

explanation.surface: The Dormouse announced he was quite satisfied.
explanation.walkthrough: In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland the Dormouse tells of three sisters living at the bottom of a well full of a sweet syrup.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dormouse's sisters live in a syrup well, so the sticky syrup is that well's contents.

parts.note: reads as a personal attendant, but means a private soldier who acts as an officer's servant

explanation.surface: A personal domestic helper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'private' looks like 'personal' but is the army rank.
explanation.definitionFit: In the British army an officer's orderly, usually a private, looks after his kit.

parts.note: reads as rent from a property, but means a sum handed over, named from the act of permitting

explanation.surface: Income from renting a property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letting' looks like renting out, but means permitting: a sum someone is allowed.
explanation.definitionFit: Pocket money or an allocated sum is what one is permitted, from the verb to allow, to let.

clue.text: Bound to make many an egotistical remark

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, standing for many
"I'm it" is a boastful claim to be the important one

explanation.surface: Someone is sure to make a lot of self-centred comments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' looks like 'sure to', but it is the noun, a boundary; 'to make' joins.
explanation.definitionFit: A bound is a boundary or ceiling, the furthest extent allowed.

explanation.surface: The collapse of a cloth-making firm.
explanation.walkthrough: Crash is a coarse linen cloth used for towels.
explanation.definitionFit: A business collapse is a smash, and coarse linen cloth goes by the name crash.

parts.note: reads as a society of poets, but means a corpse in poetic language

explanation.surface: An association of poets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body' suggests a group, but it is a dead body, in the word poets use.
explanation.definitionFit: Corse is an archaic, literary word for a corpse, a dead body.

clue.text: Medical group put in morning returning snake

indicators.note: returning means the whole combination is read backwards
put in means the medical group is placed inside the morning

parts.note: the BMA is the British Medical Association, the doctors' body

explanation.surface: Doctors' association booked in the morning to deal with a snake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put in' places the doctors' body inside the morning to make ABMAM, which 'returning' reads backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The mamba is a venomous African serpent.

explanation.surface: A verse written by a girl called Sally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sally' is not a girl but an outing; the 's means 'is'. The Excursion is a long poem by Wordsworth.
explanation.definitionFit: A sally is a jaunt or trip, and Wordsworth wrote a long verse work titled for one.

explanation.surface: Rage is on the rise.
explanation.definitionFit: To irritate someone is to vex them, and the stinging weed is a growing plant.

parts.note: reads as youngsters being jailed, but means young hares, as hare is cooked jugged in a pot

explanation.surface: Youngsters about to be locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jugged' looks like slang for jailed, but jugged hare is a stew cooked in a jug.
explanation.definitionFit: Young hares in their first year are the animals cooked in the classic jugged hare dish.
